The team has accumulated a substantial body of models, code tools, and datasets. Structural changes to the organisation, siloed working across teams, and staff churn have compounded over that time. Ownership has shifted without being formally transferred. Institutional knowledge has left with departing staff. Work has been duplicated because one team did not know another had already done it. The result is an asset base that no single person has a complete picture of, and where accountability is informal and assumed rather than defined.

This framework is a deliberate reset. It establishes clear ownership for what the team already holds, and it builds structures resilient to the conditions that caused the problem: structures that survive reorganisation, that do not depend on any one individual, and that work across team boundaries rather than within them.

It also sets the foundation for responsible adoption of new capabilities. The team is actively investigating AI and machine learning tools. Before any of those can be used in operational settings, a credible governance baseline needs to exist. This framework is that baseline.

## Purpose {#sec-framework-purpose}

This framework sets out how NFWS (National Forecasting and Warning Service) manages its data, code, and digital assets. It defines who is responsible for what, at every level, covering all assets from strategic accountability for major datasets down to day-to-day maintenance of individual code tools.

The framework operates at two levels. This document covers governance principles, roles, and standards that apply to all assets regardless of type. Companion documents cover detailed code-level guidance for tools written in each language. Where those documents are silent, this framework takes precedence. This framework does not replace or supersede existing technical guidance, such as the RTMDG, it is a guide to how we manage assets not construct them.

The Owner, Steward, and Custodian roles used throughout this framework are defined in the Data Ownership Model and Central Digital and Data Office (CDDO) roadmap 2022 to 2025, which is the top-level authority for data ownership roles and responsibilities across government. This framework applies those roles to the specific assets and working practices of the team.

This work also directly supports the team's obligations under Defra's Q-FAIR data standards aims. Q-FAIR requires that data assets are of sufficient Quality to be Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable. Rather than treating Q-FAIR compliance as a separate reporting exercise, this framework and its companion documents build it in by design. Structured asset registers make data and tools findable. Consistent file formats and schemas make them interoperable and reusable. Defined access controls and storage locations make them accessible. The tier-based quality gates and quality flags directly address the Quality dimension. Compliance is therefore a natural outcome of following the framework, not additional work on top of it.

## Scope {#sec-framework-scope}

This framework applies to all digital assets produced or consumed by in-scope NFWS teams: datasets, models, code, configuration files, documentation, and derived outputs. Companion documents define asset-specific requirements within each domain. Where a companion document does not address a particular asset type, the principles and roles in this framework apply directly.

### Teams in scope {#sec-scope-teams}

The Forecasting teams (Fluvial and Coastal Modelling, and Local Forecasting Service) and the Warning Hub teams are in scope. The Flood Forecasting Centre operates under a separate governance arrangement as a joint Met Office and Environment Agency service and is out of scope.

## Governance Roles {#sec-governance-roles}

The team uses an Owner, Steward, and Custodian model as defined in the government Data Ownership Model (CDDO, 2024). Each role has a defined grade, clear responsibilities, and can be formally delegated. These roles apply to all asset types covered by this framework, including model files, datasets, and code tools.

### Owner (Deputy Director) {#sec-owner-role}

The Owner is a senior individual with dedicated accountability for a logical grouping of data or assets and in-depth knowledge of the overall business strategy in their area. Owners hold ultimate accountability for meaning, content, quality, and distribution of their assets. They make strategic decisions about how assets are used, shared, or retired. There is one Owner per major asset or tool.

::: {.callout-note}
## Owner Grade Requirement
The CDDO Data Ownership Model recommends that Data Owners should be senior individuals but does not mandate a specific grade. The Defra Data Ownership Policy recommends SCS level. This framework requires Deputy Director grade for all Owners. This is an intentional local requirement under internal Defra group guidance and reflects the operational significance of the team's assets to Flood Incident Management.
:::

Owners are responsible for:

- Approving what data and models the team uses and produces
- Deciding who can access sensitive or nationally significant outputs
- Signing off on major changes to modelling approach, data standards, or tool promotion to Tier 3
- Resolving escalated disputes about data quality, access, or tool governance
- Ensuring the team meets organisational data governance obligations
- Understanding how assets are being used, who by, and whether they are controlled properly
- Ensuring appropriate retention schedules are in place for all data
- Ensuring their data assets comply with legal requirements for archival, disposal, and preservation
- Limiting access to data (particularly personal data or data of significance to national security) to those authorised to do so
- Ensuring security measures are in place to protect data in transit, received, or transferred to another organisation
- Considering where data assets may have value to wider government, society, and the economy, and the protection and exploitation approaches required to realise that value (see @sec-wider-value)

### Steward (Grade 7) {#sec-steward-role}

The Steward is responsible for day-to-day operational activities needed to support governance decisions made by Owners. Stewards are the operational points of contact with data expertise. They make sure standards are followed and assets are fit for purpose. Each asset or tool should have a named Steward.

Stewards are responsible for:

- Defining and maintaining data standards, naming conventions, and quality requirements
- Keeping asset registers and Tool Registers up to date
- Reviewing model quality, version control, and metadata completeness
- Approving access requests and code tool promotion between tiers
- Coordinating with Custodians to ensure good practice
- Reporting data quality issues or risks to the Owner
- Handling data governance queries and checking with the Owner for tactical guidance where needed
- Reviewing and updating this framework and the companion documents as part of annual updates
- Maintaining a data catalogue or business glossary of centralised data definitions for all assets within their domain, ensuring definitions are managed and adopted consistently across the team (see @sec-data-catalogue)
- Understanding data lineage and flow: knowing how data moves through pipelines, what transformations are applied, and the upstream and downstream impacts of any change
- Managing the data lifecycle for assets within their domain, including archival, retention review, and coordinating disposal where retention periods have expired and Owner approval has been obtained
- Working cross-functionally with stewards in adjacent teams or domains, sharing good practice and supporting resolution of cross-cutting data issues
- Assisting with periodic data maturity assessments as required by the organisation
- Periodically considering whether team data assets have value to wider government, society, or the economy, and flagging opportunities to the Owner (see @sec-wider-value)

Not all of these responsibilities carry equal weight at every tier. For Tier 1 assets, the core requirements are standards maintenance, register currency, and quality issue reporting. The fuller responsibilities (data lineage mapping, cross-functional liaison, maturity assessments, and wider value consideration) apply in proportion to asset criticality. All apply in full to Tier 3 assets.

### Custodian (Any Grade) {#sec-custodian-role}

The Custodian is responsible for capturing, storing, maintaining, and (where applicable) disposing of data and digital assets in line with the Owner's requirements. Custodians do the hands-on work: creating, running, storing, and maintaining assets correctly. They work closely with Stewards to ensure quality by executing within agreed systems according to rules and standards. Any team member can be a Custodian.

::: {.callout-note}
## Custodian Disposal Responsibility
The CDDO Data Ownership Model and Defra Data Ownership Policy both define the Custodian as responsible for "capturing, storing and disposing of data." The majority of data held by the team is observed environmental data (river flows, rainfall, water levels) which is generally retained indefinitely as it cannot be recreated and has enduring scientific and audit value. However, the disposal responsibility is included here to cover assets where retention limits do apply: superseded configuration files, deprecated tool artefacts, or data received under licence terms that include a disposal obligation. Disposal of any data requires Owner approval and must be documented.
:::

Custodians are responsible for:

- Following naming conventions, folder structures, and coding standards set by Stewards
- Using version control correctly
- Recording model run settings, tool configurations, and any issues encountered
- Flagging data quality problems or tool failures to their Steward promptly
- Not sharing assets outside agreed channels without permission
- Spotting and reporting data governance issues to the Steward
- Carrying out disposal of data or digital assets when directed by the Owner and Steward, and documenting the disposal decision, date, method, and authorisation
- Ensuring that changes to data content and controls can be audited

| Custodian | Technical expert responsible for capturing, storing, maintaining, and disposing of assets correctly. Creates, stores, and maintains assets and tools to agreed standards. Carries out disposal when authorised. Any grade. May be delegated to any team member. |

### Delegation {#sec-delegation}

Any role may be formally delegated. Delegation must be:

- Agreed between the delegating person and the delegate
- Recorded in the relevant register with a start date and end date (or noted as ongoing)
- Reviewed periodically or annually

Delegation does not transfer accountability. The original role holder remains responsible even when a role has been delegated.

For the Delegated Steward specifically: the Delegated Steward may make and record operational decisions (recommending approval or rejection of code reviews, flagging model condition ratings, and compiling audit findings) but decisions that carry governance consequences require Steward sign-off. These are: approving or rejecting a tier promotion, approving or denying an access request, signing off a condition assessment that results in a recommended suspension, and any finding that would be escalated to the Owner. The Steward remains accountable for all of these. Where the Steward and Delegated Steward disagree on a finding or recommendation, the Steward's decision takes precedence and the disagreement must be recorded in the relevant register entry.

### Relationship to the Information Asset Owner Role {#sec-iao-relationship}

The Cabinet Office IAO guidance (updated October 2025) and the Defra Data Ownership Policy both recognise the Information Asset Owner (IAO) as a distinct role focused on the security, content, quality, and distribution of information assets. The CDDO Data Ownership Model notes that organisations may wish to combine the Data Owner and IAO roles where appropriate.

Within NFWS, the Data Owner fulfils the IAO function for the team's asset domain. The Deputy Director who holds the Owner role is accountable for the information assets (databases, data stores, model repositories) that contain the team's data, as well as for the data itself. This combined accountability is appropriate given the team's structure: the same individual needs oversight of both the logical data groupings and the systems that hold them.

Where the team's data assets are held within wider organisational information assets (for example, data held within a shared Databricks environment or a centrally managed file store), the team's Data Owner coordinates with the organisational IAO for that system to ensure that access controls, security measures, and risk assessments are aligned.

The Steward acts as the operational equivalent of an Information Asset Manager (IAM), carrying out the day-to-day management responsibilities on behalf of the Owner/IAO.

The following accountabilities from the IAO guidance are explicitly held by the team's Data Owner:

- Understanding what information is held within the team's area of responsibility
- Reviewing risks to the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of information assets
- Ensuring information is appropriately protected and marked
- Inputting into the departmental information asset register
- Ensuring compliance with the Data Protection Act 2018, the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, UK GDPR, FOI and EIR regulations, and the Public Records Act
- Ensuring that any AI service has been assessed before it is allowed access to team information assets (see @sec-ai-governance)

### Asset Register Metadata Requirements {#sec-metadata-requirements}

Every data asset or tool entered in the team's registers (Tool Register, Model Register, or Hydrometric Data Register) must include metadata identifying the named individuals in each governance role. At minimum, the following must be recorded:

- **Owner**: Name, grade, and role
- **Steward**: Name, grade, and role
- **Custodian(s)**: Name(s), grade(s), and role(s)
- **IAO**: Name of the IAO (or note that the Owner fulfils this function)

This aligns with the CDDO requirement that every essential shared data asset has accurate metadata including the name and roles of responsible Data Owners and Data Steward(s), and with the Defra requirement to additionally include Custodians and IAOs.

## The Tier System {#sec-tier-system}

Not all assets carry the same risk. A script that broke at 2am during a live flood event is a different problem to one that broke during a research exercise the following week. The tier system exists to make that difference explicit, and to calibrate the governance overhead accordingly.

All team assets, whether data, models, code tools, warning configurations, or procedures, are classified into one of three tiers based on their role in live operational service. Tier 3 is operational: failure has direct consequences for the service. Tier 2 is analytical: regularly used, but not in the critical path. Tier 1 is experimental: research or prototype work, not in production. The tier determines the level of oversight required. It does not describe quality or maturity in isolation; a technically excellent piece of work begins at Tier 1 until its governance is confirmed.

The same three tiers apply to every asset type. That uniformity is deliberate. It gives the team a shared language for risk, regardless of whether the asset in question is a hydrometric dataset, a hydraulic model, a Python script, a threshold configuration, or an operational procedure.

```{mermaid}

%%| fig-width: 4

    T3["<b>Tier 3: Operational</b><br/>Live service. Failure has<br/>direct operational consequences."]
    T2["<b>Tier 2: Analytical</b><br/>Regularly used. Not in<br/>the critical forecasting path."]
    T1["<b>Tier 1: Experimental</b><br/>Research or prototype stage.<br/>Not in production."]

    T1 -->|"Promote: Owner sign-off required"| T2
    T2 -->|"Promote: Owner sign-off required"| T3

    T2 -->|"Demote: Owner sign-off required"| T1

    style T3 fill:#fdebd0,stroke:#e59866

```

| Tier | Description | Data | Models | Tools |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Tier 3:** Operational | Used in live forecasting. Failure has direct operational consequences. | Formally approved datasets feeding live model runs or supporting the service | FMP, PDM, Black Box and Boundary Conditions used in the operational forecast chain | Scripts and pipelines running in live forecasting or critical to supporting the service |
| **Tier 2:** Analytical | Regularly used but not in the critical forecasting path. | Calibration inputs, validated datasets used for post-event analysis | Models under active development or used for post-event analysis | Visualisation tools, performance dashboards, model comparison tools |
| **Tier 1:** Experimental | Research or prototype stage. Not in production. | Exploratory datasets, preliminary ingestion, unvalidated inputs | New model configurations being calibrated or tested | Research notebooks, proof-of-concept tools, ML experiments |

Promotion to Tier 3 requires Owner sign-off for all asset types. Demotion or deprecation requires Owner approval. Assets begin at Tier 1 and are promoted as their maturity and governance are confirmed. An asset must not be used in live forecasting until it has been formally promoted to Tier 3.

### Data Tiers and the Medallion Architecture {#sec-medallion-architecture}

Hydrometric data arrives from many sources and rarely arrives clean. A gauge record from the Environment Agency's API and a manually submitted spreadsheet from a partner organisation are both raw data, but they carry different levels of trust, different provenance trails, and different likelihoods of containing errors. Treating them identically at ingestion, or leaving quality decisions implicit, creates problems that compound downstream.

The medallion architecture addresses this by making quality stages explicit. Bronze is the unmodified record of what was received. Silver is the result of documented quality control. Gold is a formally approved product derived from Silver and cleared for a specific operational use. Each stage represents a distinct level of accountability. Moving data from one stage to the next requires deliberate action and a recorded decision. That is not bureaucracy; it is how the team knows what it is working with.

The medallion and the operational tier system answer different questions. The tier system asks: how critical is this asset to the live service? The medallion asks: how far has this data been through quality assurance? For code tools and models these two dimensions tend to move together. For hydrometric data they are genuinely independent, and that independence matters. The same Silver dataset might supply a Tier 2 post-event analysis today and a Tier 3 operational model run next month. The data's quality state has not changed; only its use has. Conflating the two frameworks would mean re-approving data every time its purpose changed.

The medallion architecture is not optional. Only Gold-tier data may be used as input to Tier 3 model runs or ML model training that may one day be promoted to operational use. See @sec-hydrometric-data for the full schema requirements and QC process.

### Model Tiers {#sec-model-tiers}

Flood models, including FMP hydraulic models, PDM rainfall-runoff configurations, boundary conditions, and Black Box elements, are classified under the same three-tier system. A model's tier reflects its role in the operational forecast chain, not its technical sophistication. See @sec-flood-model-governance for full details.

### Tool Tiers {#sec-tool-tiers}

Code tools written in R or Python follow the same tier system. A tool's tier reflects the operational consequences of failure. Tier 3 tools require the most rigorous development, testing, and custodianship standards. See @sec-r-governance and @sec-python-governance for language-specific requirements.

### Warning Configuration Tiers {#sec-warning-config-tiers}

Warning threshold configurations, trigger criteria, and issuance rules are classified under the same three-tier system. A configuration's tier reflects its role in live warning operations. Tier 3 configurations are those actively used in live warning issuance: an incorrect threshold either triggers a warning that should not be issued, or fails to trigger one that should. Tier 2 covers configurations under review or used for post-event threshold analysis. Tier 1 covers proposed changes being assessed against historical data before any operational use. Owner sign-off is required before a configuration can be used in live issuance. See @sec-flood-warnings for detailed standards and the Warning Configuration Register.

### Procedure Tiers {#sec-procedure-tiers}

Procedures follow the same three-tier system applied to documentary assets. The tier reflects the operational consequence of following an incorrect or outdated procedure, not its length or complexity. A procedure used during a live flood incident is Tier 3: if it is wrong, the wrong action is taken in real time. A procedure used for internal review, training, or audit is Tier 2. A draft procedure under development or consultation is Tier 1. Owner sign-off is required before a procedure is used in a live incident. See @sec-procedure-tools for the documentary review cycle and sign-off requirements.

## Asset Registers {#sec-asset-registers}

The team maintains six registers and one data catalogue. Together they answer the question no single person should have to carry in their head: what does the team hold, who is responsible for it, what state is it in, and how does it connect to everything else.

### Why Registers Are Required {#sec-registers-why}

The problems this framework was built to address (informal ownership, lost institutional knowledge, duplicated work) all share a common cause: the team's assets were not systematically recorded. Registers are the remedy. They make ownership visible, make the asset base navigable, and create the audit trail needed for accountability.

Register maintenance is not optional. The Steward is accountable for keeping all registers current. The Custodian is responsible for notifying the Steward whenever an asset changes in a way that requires a register update. An asset not recorded in the relevant register is treated as unmanaged: it may not be used in formal outputs or operational forecasting, it cannot be promoted to Tier 3, and accountability for it cannot be enforced.

| **Model Register** | All flood models (FMP, PDM, Black Box, Boundary Conditions): tier, condition ratings, calibration records | `registers/model_register.xlsx` |

: {.striped}

Each register is version-controlled. No register is edited by hand except under Steward approval. The Hydrometric Data Register is written programmatically via `reach.io`; the Tool Register is built by `scripts/build_tool_register.R`. The Model Register, Connection Register, and Warning Configuration Register are maintained by the Steward, with updates submitted by Custodians after any significant change to an asset.

Procedures are not tracked in a central register. Each team maintains a version-controlled Procedures Index in its own governance repository, listing every active procedure with its version, review date, named Owner, and sign-off record. The Steward includes procedure currency in the quarterly governance summary.

Detailed field specifications, update procedures, and the initial setup sequence for each register are in the companion documents (@sec-flood-model-governance, @sec-hydrometric-data) and in the Implementation chapter (@sec-implementation). The Tool Register is defined in full at @sec-tool-register below.

### Register Currency and Compliance {#sec-register-currency}

Every entry in any register must identify the asset's named Owner, Steward, and Custodian. The minimum metadata fields are defined at @sec-metadata-requirements.

The Steward includes register currency in the quarterly governance summary (@sec-monitoring-reporting). Registers are reviewed as part of the annual Tier 3 audit. Assets with no register entry, or with stale entries where the named Custodian has left, are escalated to the Owner for resolution.

### Cross-Asset Notification {#sec-cross-asset-notification}

When a Gold-tier dataset is superseded or a Tier 3 model's output format changes, the Steward responsible for that asset must notify any Steward whose domain depends on it. The Connection Register is the reference: any registered dependency on the changed asset creates an obligation to notify. The notified Steward must confirm with their Custodians that any affected run records, model configurations, or tool outputs are still valid. This requirement applies regardless of whether the dependency crosses language or domain boundaries.


## Asset Naming and File Standards {#sec-asset-naming}

Code tools managed in Git are versioned through commits, tags, and package metadata. Version numbers do not appear in file names. The rules for code are set out at @sec-version-control.

Complex digital assets held outside Git — model files, warning configurations, procedures, and reference datasets — follow a file-based versioning convention. Version numbers are embedded in file names because the file store itself provides no equivalent of a commit history. The register records when each version was created; the date does not belong in the file name.

### Folder structure

Every asset project must use the following layout. No ad-hoc structures. No files held solely on local machines or unmanaged drives.

```
[CatchmentID]_[Position]_[ProjectName]/
├── inputs/    — raw or processed input data
├── model/     — primary asset files
├── outputs/   — results and exported data
├── docs/      — notes, run records, calibration records, reports
└── archive/   — superseded versions
```

The `archive/` directory is the non-Git equivalent of version history. Superseded versions are moved there, never deleted. An asset that produced a formal output must remain recoverable in the exact state it was in when that output was produced.

### File naming

```
[CatchmentID]_[Position]_[AssetType]_v[MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH]
```

Examples:

| Asset | File name |
|---|---|
| FMP hydraulic model | `SEVERN_UPPER_FMP_v2.3.1` |
| PDM parameter set | `SEVERN_UPPER_Gauged_PDM_v1.4.0` |
| Warning threshold configuration | `SEVERN_UPPER_ThresholdConfig_v1.0.2` |
| Operational procedure | `SEVERN_UPPER_SevereWarningProcedure_v2.1.0` |

**Rules:** no spaces; underscores throughout; version numbers follow Semantic Versioning (MAJOR for changes that materially alter behaviour or outputs; MINOR for parameter or content updates; PATCH for corrections that do not change the substance of the asset).

Companion documents may define asset-specific variants of this convention. Where a companion document specifies a different format, that format takes precedence for assets in its scope. Where no companion document addresses a specific asset type, this convention applies by default.

## Catchment History and Condition {#sec-catchment-condition}

The tier system tells you how critical an asset is to the live service. The medallion architecture tells you how far a dataset has been through quality assurance. Neither tells you whether the asset still accurately represents the physical system it was built to describe.

That is a separate question, and it is the more fundamental one. A model may carry a high condition score and still be wrong, because the catchment it represents has changed since it was calibrated. A warning threshold may have passed Gold-tier approval and still be inappropriate, because the flow-stage relationship it depends on has since shifted. A procedure may be formally signed off and still direct responders incorrectly, because the flood defence it references no longer operates as it did.

Physical catchments change. They change suddenly through flood events. They change gradually through channel morphology, land use, and vegetation. They change deliberately through infrastructure works, gauge relocations, and rating curve revisions. Every significant change to a catchment is a potential invalidation event for every digital asset that represents it, across every team that holds one.

### Catchment change events {#sec-catchment-events}

A catchment change event is any physical or observational change that may affect the representativeness of existing digital assets for a given catchment. The following count:

- A significant flood event: one that produces flows exceeding the calibrated range of existing assets, or causes observable geomorphological change
- Construction or modification of flood defences, weirs, or control structures
- Channel modifications, major bank erosion, or in-channel works
- Relocation or replacement of a flow or stage gauge
- Revision of a rating curve used as input to operational models or warning thresholds
- Land use or vegetation change large enough to affect runoff response

No single team has full sight of all these events across a catchment. That is why the cross-team notification mechanism at @sec-cross-asset-notification exists, and why the CDT's cross-service mandate at @sec-central-data-team is structurally necessary.

### Catchment History Log {#sec-catchment-history-log}

Each team maintains a Catchment History Log for the catchments in its domain. The log records catchment change events with a date, a description of the change, and an assessment of which digital assets are affected. The Steward holds the log in the team's governance repository and reviews it as part of the quarterly governance summary (@sec-monitoring-reporting).

| Field | Description |
|---|---|
| Event date | Date the event occurred or was identified |
| Catchment | The catchment or catchments affected |
| Event type | Flood event, physical works, gauge change, rating curve revision, other |
| Description | What happened and, where known, its physical extent or significance |
| Assets affected | Asset IDs (models, datasets, thresholds, procedures) that may no longer be representative |
| Review status | Pending / Under review / Reviewed: no change required / Reviewed: update required |
| Outcome | What was done, or what is planned, for each affected asset |

: Catchment History Log fields {.striped}

### Cross-team notification {#sec-catchment-cross-notification}

When a catchment change event affects assets held by more than one team, the Steward who identifies the event must notify all other Stewards whose assets relate to that catchment. Notification must be specific: it must name the event, the catchment, and the assets the notifying Steward believes are affected in the receiving team's domain.

The receiving Steward is responsible for assessing the impact on their own assets and recording the outcome in their own log. A Steward who receives notification and takes no action is in breach of their responsibilities under this framework.

For catchments where both Forecasting and Warning teams hold operational assets, any flood event that triggers a model condition review under @sec-flood-condition-cycle also counts as a catchment change event requiring notification to the Warning Steward.

### Condition as a judgement {#sec-catchment-condition-framing}

The per-asset condition frameworks in the companion documents provide scoring criteria and required actions. They make condition judgements systematic and auditable. They are not substitutes for the judgement itself.

The flood model condition score at @sec-flood-condition answers: how fit for purpose is this model? The catchment condition concept answers the prior question: has the physical system changed in a way that requires all asset types to be reassessed, not just models? Both questions matter. The second is frequently not asked.

## Flood Model Governance {#sec-flood-model-overview}

FMP model files require formal version control because they contain binary and configuration files that change with every calibration update, boundary condition revision, or software upgrade. Both the current model and all superseded versions must be retained. A model that produced a formal output must remain recoverable in the exact state it was in when that output was produced. No FMP files may be held on local machines or unmanaged drives.

PDM parameter sets, calibration records, and coupled model configurations follow the same governance principles. Parameter sets are particularly sensitive: a set calibrated on one period of data can produce materially different outputs from a set calibrated on a different period, even for the same catchment. Version control and calibration documentation are not optional.

The detailed requirements for folder structure, naming conventions, version control, run records, condition assessment, and model connections are set out in the Flood Model Governance document (@sec-flood-model-governance). The requirements there are normative and must be followed by all Custodians working with operational models.

## Code and Tool Governance {#sec-code-tool-governance}

The team currently develops and maintains code tools in R and Python. These tools are governed by the same Owner, Steward, and Custodian framework as all other assets, with additional requirements that reflect the specific risks of code: unreproducible results, undocumented behaviour, and key-person dependency.

This section sets out the governance principles that apply to all code tools regardless of language. Detailed, language-specific standards are in @sec-r-governance and @sec-python-governance.

### Tool Classification {#sec-tool-classification}

All code tools are classified into one of three tiers based on their operational role. Governance requirements increase with tier level.

| Tier | Description | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Tier 3: Operational | Used in live forecasting; failure has direct operational consequences | Ensemble processing scripts, alert threshold tools, Flood Modeller API orchestration, operational ML inference pipelines |
| Tier 2: Analytical | Regularly used but not in the critical forecasting path | Visualisation tools, performance metrics dashboards, model comparison tools |
| Tier 1: Experimental | Research or prototype stage; not in production | New model evaluation scripts, proof-of-concept tools, ML experiments, research notebooks |

### Custodianship Requirements by Tier {#sec-custodianship-by-tier}

| Role | Tier 3: Operational | Tier 2 and 3: Analytical / Experimental |
|---|---|---|
| Owner | Deputy Director required. Must be a different individual from the Steward. | Deputy Director strongly recommended. A senior manager with equivalent accountability may be assigned where agreed with the Delegated Steward. |
| Steward | Grade 7 required. Delegated Steward recommended. | Grade 7 recommended. A capable team member at a lower grade may act as Steward for Tier 1 tools where the role is combined with Custodian. |
| Custodian | Runs scheduled CI checks, monitors for issues, escalates to Steward promptly, maintains disaster recovery runbook. | Runs tests before major language version upgrades, flags broken dependencies to Steward. |

When a team member leaves or changes role, custodianship must be formally reassigned before their departure.

### Routes to Tool Development {#sec-routes-to-development}

There are four routes by which a new tool enters the team's codebase. The route must be agreed at the point of initiation and recorded in the Tool Register.

| Route | Description | Typical Origin |
|---|---|---|
| A: New Standalone Tool | A new script or module developed from scratch. Begins at Tier 1 and may be promoted. Proposed via a Git issue; Steward confirms route and tier within five working days. | Identified gap in team capability; new forecasting requirement |
| B: Shared Module / Package Contribution | A function or class developed for inclusion in a shared package (Flode for R, shared module for Python). Follows a promotion pathway with API review by the Steward Lead. | Recurring code pattern across tools; refactoring of existing standalone tool |
| C: Adoption of External Package | An externally developed package being formally adopted for team use. Personal Tier 1 use is acceptable; shared or production use requires evaluation and sign-off. | Discovered package that meets a team need; tool shared by a partner organisation |
| D: Emergency / Hotfix | A tool or fix developed under time pressure. Verbal authorisation from the Steward required before work begins. | Forecasting failure; urgent fix required |

For Route C, all external packages must be evaluated against six criteria before adoption in shared or production code: active maintenance, compatible licence, acceptable performance impact, manageable dependency footprint, genuine necessity, and sufficient community adoption.

For Route D, no more than two emergency route deployments per twelve-month period for the same tool area is acceptable before triggering a review of the underlying operational code tools.

### Code Review Requirements {#sec-code-review-requirements}

| Tier | Review Requirement |
|---|---|
| Tier 3: Operational | Mandatory peer review by a second team member before merging to main. Senior reviewer sign-off before first production deployment. Annual audit of all Tier 3 tools. |
| Tier 2: Analytical | Peer review required before merging to main. Reviewer must have at least intermediate proficiency in the relevant language. |
| Tier 1: Experimental | Self-review checklist minimum. Peer review strongly encouraged before sharing with others. |

### Version Control Principles {#sec-version-control}

All code tools used by more than one person must be managed in Git. No shared tool may exist solely on a local machine or shared drive.

**Branching:** the team follows a simplified Git Flow model: `main` (production-ready only, no direct commits), `develop` (integration branch), `feature/<n>` (individual work), `hotfix/<n>` (urgent fixes to Tier 3), `release/<version>` (versioned releases).

**Commits:** all commits must follow the Conventional Commits convention `<type>(<scope>): <short description>` with a body explaining why, not just what. Permitted types: `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `refactor`, `test`, `chore`.

**Versioning:** all tools and packages follow Semantic Versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH). The version number is recorded in three places: the Git release tag (e.g. `v2.1.0`), the `CHANGELOG.md` entry, and the package metadata file (`DESCRIPTION` for R, `pyproject.toml` for Python). It is never appended to a file name. A file called `process_data.R` must not become `process_data_v2.1.0.R`. The commit history and release tags are the version record. Embedding versions in file names duplicates that record, creates ambiguity, and breaks as soon as files are moved or renamed.

**Reproducibility:** all dependencies must be pinned and committed alongside the code: `renv.lock` for R tools, `poetry.lock` for Python tools. Code must be runnable from a clean environment without undeclared dependencies.

**Releases:** a release is a named, tagged point in the commit history. To cut a release: merge the `release/<version>` branch to `main`, tag the commit (`git tag -a v2.1.0 -m "Release v2.1.0"`), push the tag (`git push origin v2.1.0`), and update `CHANGELOG.md` on `develop`. No files are renamed. The tag is the version marker.

::: {.callout-note}
## File naming versus Git versioning
These rules apply to **code tools managed in Git**. Model files (FMP, PDM, boundary conditions) are not code and are typically held on shared drives rather than in a Git repository. For those assets, version numbers in file names are the appropriate convention. See @sec-flood-file-standards for model file naming rules.
:::


### Tool Register {#sec-tool-register}

Every code tool must be entered in the central Tool Register at the point it is shared with more than one team member. The register is a CSV file (`tool_register.csv`) held in this governance repository and generated by `scripts/build_tool_register.R`. It is not edited by hand.

The script works in two passes. First, it queries the GitHub API for all repositories in the `JonPayneEA` organisation and extracts the fields GitHub holds natively: repository name, URL, primary language, and topics. Second, for each repository it reads a `governance.yml` file from the repository root, which supplies the governance fields GitHub cannot know. Values in `governance.yml` take precedence over inferred values; GitHub topics are used as a fallback for tier and status.

A template `governance.yml` is provided in this repository at `governance-template.yml`. Every tool repository must include a populated copy in its root. Two GitHub topic conventions are required on every tool repository, and used as fallback when `governance.yml` is absent or incomplete:

- Tier: one of `tier-3`, `tier-2`, `tier-1`
- Status: one of `active`, `under-development`, `deprecated`

The resulting register fields are:

| Field | Source |
|---|---|
| Tool Name | GitHub repository name |
| Tier | `governance.yml` → GitHub topic |
| Language | `governance.yml` → GitHub detected language |
| Status | `governance.yml` → GitHub topic |
| Owner (name, grade) | `governance.yml` |
| Steward (name, grade, delegation) | `governance.yml` |
| Custodian(s) | `governance.yml` |
| IAO | `governance.yml` |
| Repository Location | GitHub repository URL |
| Last Reviewed | `governance.yml` |
| Notes | `governance.yml` → GitHub repository description |

The register must be regenerated whenever a custodianship role changes, a tool changes tier, or a tool is deprecated. Run `Rscript scripts/build_tool_register.R` and commit the updated `tool_register.csv`.

### Handover and Succession {#sec-handover-succession}

When a Steward or Custodian changes, the outgoing person must produce a handover note before they leave. The note covers: the tool's purpose and known quirks, current technical debt or open issues, the status of any open pull requests, and scheduled maintenance tasks. It is stored in the tool's `docs/` directory.

For Tier 3 tools, the incoming Steward must run the full test suite and confirm it passes before formally accepting the handover. The Delegated Steward must be notified of all Tier 3 custodianship changes.

## Data Catalogue and Centralised Definitions {#sec-data-catalogue}

The Steward is responsible for maintaining a data catalogue or business glossary that records centralised definitions for the team's key data entities, attributes, and terminology. This aligns with the CDDO Data Ownership Model requirement that agreed data definitions be maintained through Data Stewards.

The data catalogue should cover at minimum:

- Definitions for the team's core data types (flow, stage, rainfall, catchment descriptors) and what each means in the team context
- The relationship between supplier terminology and team terminology (for example, mapping supplier quality codes to the team's flag scheme)
- Definitions for key model parameters and what they represent physically
- Naming conventions for datasets, tools, and models, consolidated from across the governance suite

The catalogue is maintained by the Steward and reviewed as part of the annual governance audit. It may take the form of a structured document, a spreadsheet, or a dedicated section within the team's internal documentation site.

## Data Quality {#sec-data-quality}

Data quality is everyone's responsibility. The following minimum standards apply to all datasets.

| Standard | What it means | Who checks it |
|---|---|---|
| Accuracy | Data reflects reality; values are plausible and within expected ranges | Custodian (initial), Steward (sign-off) |
| Completeness | No unexplained gaps; missing data is flagged and documented | Custodian |
| Consistency | Same datasets used consistently across models in the same study | Steward |
| Timeliness | Input data is current enough for the model's intended purpose | Steward |
| Traceability | Every input can be traced back to its source | Custodian |
| Reproducibility | Anyone with access to the inputs and model should get the same outputs | Steward or Custodian (audit) |

## Access and Sharing {#sec-access-sharing}

- All team members have read access to current model files by default
- Write access to master model files requires Steward approval; approval is recorded in the access log with the name of the person, the date, and the scope of access granted
- Sharing data or tools outside the team (including to contractors) requires Owner approval
- Sensitive datasets follow the organisation's data classification policy
- Access rights are reviewed by Stewards every six months

## Data Incidents and Escalation {#sec-data-incidents}

A data incident is any event that affects the integrity, availability, or confidentiality of team assets including accidental deletion, use of wrong input data in a published output, tool failure in a live operational forecast environment, or unauthorised sharing.

When an incident occurs:

- The Custodian reports it to the Steward immediately
- All incidents are recorded in the governance log with a summary of what happened and what was done
- The Steward escalates to the Owner immediately where the incident affects a formal output, an external stakeholder, or carries potential regulatory or reputational implications; for all other incidents, the Steward uses their judgement

For any Tier 3 asset failure or emergency deployment (Route D), a post-incident review must be completed within ten working days. The review covers: what happened, what the impact was or could have been, what was done to resolve it, and what change is needed to prevent recurrence. The Steward is responsible for completing the review and submitting it to the Owner.

## Monitoring, Reporting, and Risk Management {#sec-monitoring-reporting}

The CDDO Data Ownership Model requires that ownership policies include monitoring and reporting arrangements as part of the organisation's broader risk management practices. The following cadence applies:

**Quarterly:** The Steward produces a governance summary covering: data quality trends from the Hydrometric Data Framework quarterly summaries, open Data Quality Issue Log entries and their age, Tool Register and Model Register currency, any incidents or near-misses in the quarter, and supplier engagement outcomes. This summary is shared with the Owner and feeds into the team's quarterly governance review.

**Annually:** The Delegated Steward conducts a full governance audit of all Tier 3 assets (code tools, models, and data). Findings are compiled into an annual governance report, which is presented to the Owner and submitted to the organisational risk management process. The report covers: compliance rates across all Tier 3 assets, condition rating trends for models, test coverage and documentation currency for tools, data quality trends, and any governance exceptions granted during the year.

**On occurrence:** Data incidents, governance exceptions, and emergency deployments (Route D) are reported to the Steward immediately and to the Owner where they affect formal outputs. Patterns of recurring incidents or exceptions are flagged in the quarterly summary and, if persistent, escalated to the organisation's risk register.

**Non-compliance.** Where the annual audit identifies assets that do not meet the requirements of this framework, the Delegated Steward produces a corrective action plan within one month of the audit report. The plan specifies the gap, the required action, the responsible Custodian or Steward, and a target date. Assets with outstanding corrective actions are flagged in the quarterly summary until resolved. Persistent or repeated non-compliance with Tier 3 requirements is escalated to the Owner and documented in the governance log. An asset that has failed to meet a corrective action target without documented justification must not be used in a new formal output until the gap is resolved.

The Owner is responsible for ensuring that governance findings are communicated to the broader organisational governance and risk management structures as appropriate.

## Wider Data Value {#sec-wider-value}

The CDDO Data Ownership Model requires organisations to consider where data assets may have value to wider government, society, and the economy. The Steward should periodically (at least annually, as part of the governance review) consider whether any of the team's data assets, particularly Gold-tier hydrometric data, model validation datasets, or calibration benchmarks, could have value to other Defra teams, other government departments, academic researchers, or the public.

Where an opportunity is identified, the Steward flags it to the Owner with a brief assessment of the data's potential value, any licensing or access constraints, and any preparation work that would be needed. The Owner decides whether to pursue sharing, taking account of supplier licence terms, data sensitivity, and resource implications.

This does not create an obligation to share all data. It creates an obligation to ask the question.

## AI and Machine Learning Governance {#sec-ai-governance}

The team uses AI and ML tools in two ways: commercial or external services that may access team data, and internally developed ML models that feed operational forecasts. Both require governance. Neither is well-served by ad-hoc decisions.

**Assessment before access.** Before any AI or ML service is given access to team data, the Steward must assess three things: what data the service will access and at what tier, whether that data contains personal or sensitive information requiring a DPIA, and whether the service complies with government Secure by Design principles. The assessment is a short written record, approved by the Owner and stored alongside the relevant Tool Register entry or dataset provenance record. This applies equally to commercial tools (such as Microsoft Copilot or cloud inference APIs) and to internally developed inference pipelines.

**ML models in operational use.** Any ML model whose outputs feed Tier 3 forecasts is itself a Tier 3 asset. It must have a named Custodian, a training dataset recorded as a Gold product (see @sec-hydrometric-data), version-controlled model artefacts with a JSON metadata file, and a formal condition assessment on the Tier 3 review schedule. The Python governance document (@sec-python-governance) sets out the technical requirements for training and inference separation, metadata files, and ONNX archiving.

**Run record requirements.** For any ML model used in an operational forecast, the run record must identify the model version, the training dataset version, and any known limitations. Where an ML model replaces a physically-based model, the replacement decision must be documented, comparative performance evidence provided, and the change approved by the Owner before deployment.

The Steward monitors developments in AI legislation and government guidance that affect the team's use of ML tools. This is reviewed as part of the annual governance audit.

## Review and Compliance {#sec-review-compliance}

This framework and the companion documents are reviewed annually by the Stewards (or subject matter experts), with Owner sign-off. The review considers:

- Whether the asset categories and roles are still fit for purpose
- Any incidents or near-misses from the previous year
- Changes to tools, data sources, or organisational requirements
- Feedback from Custodians on what is working and what is not
- Alignment with any updates to the CDDO Data Ownership Model, Defra Data Ownership Policy, IAO guidance, or relevant legislation

The Delegated Steward conducts an annual audit of all Tier 3 code tools, covering header block completeness, test coverage, documentation currency, dependency lockfile consistency, and branching strategy compliance.

Stewards must carry out spot-check audits of Tier 2 model files and metadata records at least once per year, and of Tier 1 assets at least once every two years. Spot checks may be carried out at any time.

### Framework Version Control {#sec-version-control-framework}

Changes to this document and the companion documents fall into three categories.

**Editorial corrections** are typos, broken links, or formatting fixes that do not change meaning. The Delegated Steward may make and merge editorial corrections at any time without Owner sign-off. No version increment. No team notification required, though the change is visible in the git history.

**Substantive changes** are anything that changes a requirement, adds or removes a role, adds or removes a process step, or modifies a companion document in a way that affects practice. Substantive changes require Owner sign-off before they are merged. The minor version number increments (1.4 becomes 1.5). The Steward notifies the team by written summary within five working days of the merge, identifying which sections changed and why.

**Major changes** are restructures of the tier system, redefinition of core roles, or changes that require existing registers to be migrated or existing assets to be re-assessed. Major changes trigger a full review cycle and increment the major version number (1.4 becomes 2.0). They are treated the same as a new framework adoption.

For all substantive and major changes, the procedure is:

1. Draft the change on a branch
2. Record the rationale in the Change Log in Appendix D before requesting sign-off
3. Obtain Owner sign-off
4. Merge and increment the version number in `_quarto.yml` (master) and in the metadata block of the changed document
5. Update the review dates in any companion documents that reference the changed section

The version field in `_quarto.yml` is the master. All companion document metadata blocks reference it and must be kept in step.

### Owner Annual Engagement Requirement {#sec-owner-engagement}

Owner sign-off on the annual review is not a formality. Before signing, the Owner must be able to confirm each of the following:

- I can name the Tier 3 assets in my domain and identify their named Custodian.
- I have read the most recent quarterly governance summary produced by the Steward.
- I am aware of the current condition ratings for Tier 3 models in my domain and have been briefed on any asset rated Requires Attention or below.
- I have reviewed and approved any Tier 3 promotions, Gold dataset approvals, or exception requests raised during the review period.
- I am aware of any open incidents or escalated quality issues from the previous year and their resolution status.

Where the Owner cannot confirm one or more of these, the Steward must provide a briefing before sign-off is given. This is not a barrier to adoption; it is the minimum engagement the role requires.

## Quick Reference: Who to Go To {#sec-quick-reference}

| Question or task | Go to |
|---|---|
| I need access to a dataset, model file, or code tool | Steward |
| I want to share data, a model, or a tool externally | Steward (assessment), Owner (approval) |
| I've found a data quality problem | Steward |
| I want to propose a new code tool | Custodian to Steward or Delegated Steward; raise a Git issue |
| I want to adopt an external package for production use | Custodian to Steward or Delegated Steward; see R or Python companion doc |
| I need to know if a tool version is approved for Tier 3 use | Steward |
| A Tier 3 tool has failed during a live forecast | Steward immediately, then Owner; follow Route D |
| I've made a mistake that affected a published output | Steward immediately, then Owner depending on scale of issue |
| I want to change the governance framework or a companion document | Steward (draft), Owner (approval) |
| I want to give an AI tool access to team data | Steward (assessment), Owner (approval) |
| My role is unclear or there's a dispute | Steward, Owner |
